lede: Eleven organs, two journeys. A sperm travels out of the body; an ovum travels in towards the uterus. Learn each journey once and the names, and the job of every name, come free with it.
can: Name every part of both systems on an exam diagram, and spell urethra so it is not read as ureter.
Give the function of each part in the verb the mark scheme is reading for.
Say where fertilisation happens, where the embryo implants, and which organ makes which hormone.

md: Two sets of organs, each built for one journey: a sperm travelling out of the body, an ovum travelling in towards the uterus. Learn the journey and the names come with it.

md:
**1.** Sperm are made in the **testis**, which hangs in the **scrotum** outside the body.
**2.** The **sperm tube** carries them away from the testis.
**3.** The **prostate gland** adds fluid; sperm plus that fluid is **semen**.
**4.** The semen leaves along the **urethra**, which runs through the **penis**.

The prostate gland is the junction: sperm tube before it, urethra after it.

prompt: In the male reproductive system, the tube that carries sperm away from the testis is called the ______ ______.
answer: sperm tube | sperm duct | vas deferens
explain: The sperm tube. CCEA prints 'sperm tube'; other books call it the vas deferens, and either is accepted, but write the one on the specification.

title: Why the scrotum hangs outside
md:
Sperm are made best at a temperature a little **below** body temperature, so the testes are kept outside the body cavity where it is cooler. That is the whole reason, and it is worth a mark on its own.

One warning about the **urethra**. It is the only tube in the body that carries semen at one time and urine at another — but never both at once. Nothing else here touches urine: urine is made in the **kidney** and carried down by the **ureter**, which is a different tube with an almost identical name.

prompt: What does the prostate gland do?
explain: It adds fluid to the sperm, and sperm plus that fluid is semen. Answers to this question drift towards urine more than anything else on the paper.

md:
**1.** The **ovary** releases one **ovum**, about once a month.
**2.** The **oviduct** catches it in its fringed funnel and carries it along. **This is where fertilisation happens.**
**3.** The ovum reaches the **uterus**, whose thick lining is where an embryo could settle.

Below the uterus is the **cervix**, a ring of muscle, and below that the **vagina**.

title: Other books, other names
md:
Other books call the sperm tube the **vas deferens** and the oviduct the **Fallopian tube**. Same structures. CCEA prints **sperm tube** and **oviduct**, so write those.

The **epididymis**, the **seminal vesicles**, **FSH** and **LH** belong to other specifications, not this one.

prompt: In which part of the female reproductive system does fertilisation take place?
explain: The oviduct. The ovum is fertilised on its way from the ovary to the uterus; the uterus is where the ball of cells settles afterwards.

title: Worked example: 'Give the function of the parts labelled C and D. [2]'
md:
**Step 1 — read the command word.** It asks for the **function**, not the name.
**Step 2 — C is the tube leaving the testis**: it *carries sperm away from the testis*. **[1]**
**Step 3 — D is the gland around the top of the urethra**: it *adds fluid to the sperm to make semen*. **[1]**
**Step 4 — check.** Neither answer mentions urine.

title: Why step 4 is there
md: Summer 2024: answers for the **prostate gland** and the testis **centred on urine**. Naming the structures was not asked for, and a name that missed cost the mark.

title: KS3 Biology - Human Reproductive Systems
why: A short second pass over both systems, now that you have been through them once. The uploader calls it KS3 because in England this is taught before GCSE; in CCEA Double Award Science it is examinable B2 content, so it is the right level for you.

prompt: Which organ makes the hormone oestrogen?
answer: ovary | the ovary | ovaries | the ovaries
explain: The ovary. It releases ova and makes oestrogen, which is why an anatomy question can ask you to name a hormone.

Divide by the magnification; never multiply.</text><text x="108" y="113" text-anchor="end" font-size="11.5">on the page</text><text x="108" y="205" text-anchor="end" font-size="11.5">real length</text><text x="468" y="158" font-size="11.5">÷ 0.5, which doubles it</text><text x="120" y="142" font-size="11">55 mm measured with a ruler</text><text x="120" y="234" font-size="11">110 mm in the body</text></g></svg>
caption: The page is the short bar. The body is the long one.

md:
Diagrams in books are printed at a **scale**. Half life size means the drawing is half as long as the real thing, so the real thing is **twice** the drawing.

An oviduct measures 55 mm on a diagram printed at half life size. Real length = drawn ÷ magnification = 55 ÷ 0.5 = 110 mm, which is 11.0 cm.

Divide, never multiply, when the drawing is smaller than the real thing — and read the unit on the answer line.

prompt: A uterus measures 40 mm across on a diagram printed at half life size. How wide is it really, in millimetres?
explain: 40 ÷ 0.5 = 80 mm. Half life size means the real thing is twice the drawing.

md:
Name all six parts of the **male** system and all five of the **female** system on a diagram.
Give the **function** of each one in the words the scheme uses.
Spell **urethra** so it cannot be read as ureter, and keep urine out of every answer.
Say that fertilisation happens in the **oviduct**, that the embryo implants in the **uterus lining**, and which organ makes **oestrogen** and which makes **testosterone**.
Turn a length on a scaled diagram into a real length, with the right unit.

This is the settling-in question at the front of the paper, about **five marks**. The first mark is almost always a structure named off a diagram; the last is a function. Stuck on a function? Give the **verb** — what it makes, carries, adds or holds — and leave the name out unless you are sure of it, because a name that misses, written beside a right function, costs the mark.
